docs.title: Why TestBudget
docs.text:
A pull request does not need every test. But running only some of them is a gamble, and nobody can say how risky it is.

TestBudget turns that gamble into a measured budget. It learns from your CI history which tests fail, and which source files they fail with. For a new change it ranks the tests by how much risk they cover per second, then runs as many as fit the time budget you choose, and says why each one was picked or skipped.

The claim we test: running 30% of the suite catches at least 85% of failing runs. The method for checking it is in the evaluation protocol, and results are reported as they come out, including if they miss.

python -m testbudget.cli init
python -m testbudget.cli ingest fixtures/sample_junit.xml
python -m testbudget.cli plan --changed src/checkout.py --budget 30

Next: link tests to the code they cover, or browse the API reference.

docs.text: This page lists which AI tools were used on TestBudget, what they were used for, and how a human checked the output.

All four members used the same two tools: Claude and ChatGPT, through their normal chat apps. Exact model versions were not recorded for ChatGPT. The teammate rows below were reported by Namrata, and each member can correct their own row by pull request.

docs.title: Prompts and plans
docs.text:
The AI chats for this track were held in the Claude and ChatGPT apps and are not stored as files in this repository. Prompt transcripts or agent plan files that other members committed can be found with:

git ls-files | grep -i -E "prompt|plan|transcript|agent"

docs.title: How a human checked the AI's output
docs.text:
Every AI-written change followed the same rules. It was run locally with python -m pytest -q before being committed, and it went through a pull request that another member reviews before merge. Reviews of PRs #45 and #46 are on those pull requests.

Specific examples:

  1. Bug found by running the code. The first version of summarize_links crashed with AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get' when run against the older fixtures/test_links.json, whose entries are plain strings, not objects. This was found by running python -m testbudget.cli links --report by hand. The fix and its tests are in the commits "fix(links): make report tolerate legacy string entries and non-object JSON" and "test(links): cover legacy entries and non-object JSON" in PR #46.
  2. Environment check. The project requires Python 3.10 or newer, but the local virtual environment used Python 3.9. This was noticed when pip install -e failed. The new code was checked with the existing 20 tests plus the new ones under the local interpreter, and a proper Python 3.10+ environment is still needed for the full install.
  3. Assumptions flagged, not hidden. The format of the pins section in testbudget.yml (a mapping from test ID to a list of files) was an assumption in the AI-written code. It is raised as a comment on PR #45 for the owner of testbudget.yml to confirm.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: AI-written code can be confidently wrong. We treat it like code from any other contributor: it needs tests, a reviewer, and a passing CI run before it reaches main.

docs.title: rank_tests(stats, changed_files, links)
docs.text: Rank tests using a simple baseline score. Inputs: stats: Historical statistics produced by db.get_test_stats() changed_files: List of source files changed in the pull request. links: Mapping of source files to related tests. Current baseline scoring: +10 if test is linked to changed code +5 for each historical failure Then divide by average runtime. This favors tests that are: - relevant to the current change - historically failure-prone - relatively inexpensive to run This is the initial baseline ranker, not the final TestBudget research ranking algorithm.

docs.title: rank_tests_coverage(stats, changed_files, links, file_weights)
docs.text:
Rank tests by greedy budgeted maximum coverage of the changed files.

Each test covers the changed files linked to it. A file is worth 1 + file_weights.get(file, 0). The test with the largest uncovered value per second (duration floored at 0.1 s) is picked next, then the files it covers keep 0.3 of their remaining value. Tests that cover no changed file go last, most recent failure first (last_failure, an ISO timestamp, if the stats carry it), then by name. Ties break by name. Args: stats: Historical statistics, as db.get_test_stats returns. changed_files: Source files changed in the pull request. links: Mapping of source file to linked test names. file_weights: Failure weight per file, e.g. from riskmap.file_failure_weights. Returns: Ranked tests in the shape rank_tests returns; score is the value per second at the moment the test was picked.

docs.title: testbudget.selector
docs.text: Budget cut over a ranked, rule-ordered test list.

docs.title: select_with_budget(ranked_tests, budget)
docs.text:
Select ranked tests while staying within the supplied time budget.

Forced tests (forced=True, set by the hard rules) are always selected and their duration counts against the budget first, even past it. The remaining tests are considered in ranking order; a test that does not fit is skipped, and later shorter tests may still be selected. Args: ranked_tests: Ranked tests with duration and optional forced. budget: Time budget in seconds. Returns: {"selected", "skipped", "estimated_runtime", "budget"}; selected tests keep ranking order, skipped tests carry skip_reason. Raises: ValueError: If budget is negative.

docs.title: select_with_rules(ranked_tests, budget, context)
docs.text:
Apply the hard rules, then cut the result to the budget.

Pinned, rotation-limit and full-suite tests are forced: they count against the budget but are never cut.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ranked_tests Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]]

Output of ranker.rank_tests.

required budget float

Time budget in seconds.

required context RuleContext

Rule context (config, changed files, history, ref).

required

Returns: select_with_budget output plus run_all and trigger from rules.apply_rules. Raises: ValueError: If budget is negative or the rule inputs are malformed.

docs.title: 1. Hypothesis
docs.text:
TestBudget, run with a time budget of 30% of the full suite's duration, catches at least 85% of historically failing runs. A run is caught if at least one test that failed in that run is in the selected set.

This claim is written before any result exists. Results are reported as they come out, including if they miss.

docs.title: 2. Baselines
docs.text:
TestBudget is compared with these orderings, all given the same history and the same budget:

  1. Original order: tests in the order the suite runs them today.
  2. Random: a seeded random order, repeated over several seeds and averaged.
  3. pytest-ranking, three heuristics: recently failed first, most often failed first, and most recently modified first.
  4. Import-only: tests whose files import a changed file, with no history.

docs.title: 3. Metrics
docs.text:
• Catch rate at 30% of suite time: share of failing runs where a failing test falls inside the selected set, with selected tests totalling at most 30% of the full suite duration.
  • APFDc: cost-aware average percentage of faults detected, where each test costs its duration.
  • Time to first failure: seconds of test time before the first failing test runs in a failing run.

Each metric is reported per method and per risk level.

docs.title: 4. Temporal split
docs.text: Runs are replayed in the order they happened. The plan for run N uses only runs 1 to N-1: their results, their changed files and the skip debt they left. Nothing from run N or later is read. A test enforces this.

docs.title: 5. Failing runs and flakes
docs.text: A failing run is a run where at least one test has status failed or error after retries. A failure is flaky, and is dropped from the failing set, if the same test passes on retry or passes on the same SHA in another attempt. Until the flake filter module exists, this one-line rule is used. Runs that fail on installation or collection are recorded but not counted as test failures.

docs.title: 6. Failure conditions
docs.text:
The hypothesis fails if any of these hold on the committed history:

  • catch rate at 30% of suite time is below 85%
  • TestBudget is not above the best baseline at the same budget
  • there are too few failing runs to say anything (fewer than about 10 per risk level)

A fail is reported in the M0 issue with the number, the commit it was computed at, and one decision: persevere, re-plan or descope.

docs.title: 7. Data sources
docs.text:
• MealSlot CI history, back-filled from GitHub Actions. Most artifacts will have expired, so most runs are rebuilt by checking out each commit and running the suite.
  • One public pytest repository chosen for frequent CI and real test failures.
  • Any planted failures are labelled synthetic and reported separately from real ones.

docs.title: Flake filtering
docs.text:
TestBudget uses historical failures to estimate risk and evaluate whether a budgeted plan would have caught past failures.

Flaky failures can distort both calculations.

The flake filter therefore derives whether historical failures should count as real failures.

docs.title: What is a flaky failure?
docs.text:
TestBudget marks a failed result as flaky when the same test passes on the same Git SHA.

The same SHA matters because it means the code under test did not change.

docs.title: Pass on retry
docs.text:
Example:

SHA: abc123
Test: tests/test_cart.py::test_cart

attempt 1: failed
attempt 2: passed

The failed attempt is marked:

{
  "flaky": true,
  "flake_reason": "passed_on_retry"
}

The passing record remains a passing record.

docs.title: Pass on the same SHA
docs.text:
A test may also be executed more than once against the same commit without being represented as numbered retry attempts.

Example:

SHA: abc123

execution A:
test_cart = failed

execution B:
test_cart = passed

The failure is marked:

{
  "flaky": true,
  "flake_reason": "passed_on_same_sha"
}

Because identical code produced both a pass and a failure, TestBudget treats the failure as nondeterministic.

docs.title: Different SHA does not count
docs.text:
This is not considered flaky:

abc123:
test_cart = failed

def456:
test_cart = passed

The passing result belongs to different code.

The failure on abc123 therefore remains a real historical failure.

docs.title: Different test does not count
docs.text:
A pass must have the same test_id.

A passing login test does not make a failing checkout test flaky even when both were executed on the same SHA.

docs.title: Derived data
docs.text:
Flake information is not added to:

history/results.jsonl

The JSONL history remains the canonical source of observed facts.

Flake classification is calculated when history is analyzed.

This keeps the committed history reproducible and avoids rewriting historical records as the flake policy evolves.

docs.title: Using the filter
docs.text:
from testbudget.flakes import (
    mark_flaky_failures,
)

marked = mark_flaky_failures(results)

Each returned result contains:

flaky
flake_reason

For example:

{
  "sha": "abc123",
  "test_id": "tests/test_cart.py::test_cart",
  "status": "failed",
  "duration_s": 1.4,
  "attempt": 1,
  "flaky": true,
  "flake_reason": "passed_on_retry"
}

The input records are not modified.

docs.title: Filtering real failures
docs.text:
Evaluation code can use:

from testbudget.flakes import (
    filter_non_flaky_failures,
)

failures = filter_non_flaky_failures(results)

This returns only failures that remain after flake filtering.

Member 2's data-check and temporal replay can use this helper before calculating failing-run counts and catch rate.

docs.title: Playwright retry records
docs.text:
The Playwright adapter may already collapse a retried test into one final logical result.

For example:

{
  "status": "passed",
  "attempt": 2
}

Such a record is not a historical failure, so it is naturally excluded by filter_non_flaky_failures.

docs.title: Failure cases
docs.text:
The flake filter rejects malformed history, including:

  • missing required fields;
  • empty SHA values;
  • empty test IDs;
  • unsupported statuses;
  • negative durations;
  • non-positive attempt numbers.

Invalid history is rejected rather than silently changing evaluation results.

docs.title: Migrating prototype history
docs.text:
TestBudget's first prototype stored historical test executions in a local SQLite database.

The current format uses committed JSONL history:

  • history/runs.jsonl
  • history/results.jsonl

The migration utility converts prototype databases into the current format.

docs.title: Run the migration
docs.text:
From the repository root:

```bash python -m testbudget.migrate \ --db testbudget.db \ --history-dir history

docs.title: TestBudget History
docs.text:
TestBudget stores CI history as append-only JSONL files committed to the repository.

The JSONL files are the persistent source of truth. SQLite is rebuilt from those files when TestBudget needs to query historical data.

docs.title: Why JSONL?
docs.text:
The original TestBudget prototype stored history in a local SQLite database.

That worked for the first vertical slice, but a local database is difficult to review, merge, reproduce, and share through Git.

The JSONL format makes history:

  • visible in Git;
  • append-only;
  • reproducible from a clean clone;
  • usable by replay and calibration;
  • mergeable across development branches.

docs.title: Run history
docs.text:
history/runs.jsonl contains one JSON object per recorded CI run.

Example:

```json { "sha": "abc123", "timestamp": "2026-10-21T12:00:00Z", "branch": "main", "changed_files": [ "src/cart.py", "src/payment.py" ] }

Fields: - sha: Git commit SHA for the run. - timestamp: timestamp for the run. - branch: branch associated with the run. - changed_files: files changed by the commit or pull request. A SHA may appear only once in runs.jsonl. Test result history history/results.jsonl contains one JSON object per test attempt. Example: { "sha": "abc123", "test_id": "tests/test_cart.py::test_add_item", "status": "passed", "duration_s": 1.25, "attempt": 1 }

Fields: - sha: run SHA that owns this result. - test_id: stable TestBudget test identity. - status: passed, failed, or skipped. - duration_s: execution time in seconds. - attempt: retry attempt number beginning at 1. A result must reference a SHA present in runs.jsonl. Rebuilding SQLite Applications should not treat a .db file as persistent history. Load the committed history using: from testbudget.db import rebuild_history_dbconnection = rebuild_history_db("history")

The returned SQLite connection contains: - runs - results For example: rows = connection.execute( "SELECT test_id, status FROM results").fetchall()

The database exists only as the query layer. The JSONL files remain the source of truth. Historical test statistics Per-test statistics can be obtained with: from testbudget.db import get_history_test_statsstats = get_history_test_stats("history")

docs.title: How to: link tests to source files
docs.text: TestBudget decides what to run using links: which source files each test depends on. There are four sources: import, route, cofail and pin.

docs.title: Build import links for a Python project
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from testbudget.links.imports import build_import_links
from testbudget.links.writer import write_links

links = build_import_links(Path("."))
write_links(links, "links.json")

Each test file is parsed with ast; imports that resolve to files inside the repository become links with source: "import". A file that cannot be parsed is skipped with a warning instead of stopping the run.

docs.title: Add links from past failures
docs.text:
from testbudget.links.cofail import build_cofail_links, read_jsonl
from testbudget.links.writer import merge_links, write_links

runs = read_jsonl("history/runs.jsonl")
results = read_jsonl("history/results.jsonl")
write_links(merge_links(links, build_cofail_links(runs, results)), "links.json")

Files changed on commits where a test failed become weighted links to that test, scaled so the strongest link has weight 1.0.

docs.title: Inspect the result
docs.text:
python -m testbudget.cli links --report --links links.json

LINKS REPORT
--------------------------------
Tests: 4
  with links:    4
  without links: 0
Total links: 7
By source:
  import: 7

See the API reference for every function.

docs.title: Playwright adapter
docs.text:
TestBudget's Playwright adapter converts Playwright test results and TestBudget plans into the shared TestBudget formats.

It provides two main capabilities:

  1. normalize Playwright JUnit results into TestBudget history;
  2. group selected Playwright tests into per-file invocation lists.

docs.title: Test identity
docs.text:
Playwright tests use:

file › title

Example:

tests/checkout.spec.ts › checkout rejects an invalid card

This identity is shared by history, links, ranking, replay, and execution.

docs.title: Generating Playwright JUnit
docs.text:
Playwright can write a JUnit report using:

PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_NAME=results.xml \
npx playwright test --reporter=junit

For TestBudget retry information, configure the JUnit reporter with retry details enabled.

For example:

import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    [
      'junit',
      {
        outputFile: 'results.xml',
        includeRetries: true,
      },
    ],
  ],
});

The same behavior can also be enabled through Playwright's JUnit retry environment option.

docs.title: Parsing JUnit
docs.text:
from testbudget.adapters.playwright_adapter import (
    parse_playwright_junit,
)

results = parse_playwright_junit("results.xml")

A normal result looks like:

{
  "test_id": "tests/checkout.spec.ts › checkout succeeds",
  "status": "passed",
  "duration_s": 1.2,
  "attempt": 1
}

docs.title: Status normalization
docs.text:
TestBudget uses:

passed
failed
skipped

JUnit failure and error records become:

failed

Skipped records become:

skipped

docs.title: Retry deduplication
docs.text:
A retried Playwright test counts as one logical test.

Suppose:

attempt 1: failed, 1.4 seconds
attempt 2: passed, 0.8 seconds

TestBudget stores:

{
  "status": "passed",
  "duration_s": 0.8,
  "attempt": 2
}

The important points are:

  • the test appears once;
  • the final outcome is stored;
  • the final attempt's duration is stored;
  • the attempt number preserves the fact that retrying occurred.

The later flake filter uses retry information to classify flaky failures.

docs.title: Older Playwright classnames
docs.text:
Some Playwright JUnit versions may include source locations:

tests/login.spec.ts:13:5

TestBudget removes the unstable line and column suffix:

tests/login.spec.ts

This keeps the test ID stable when source lines move.

docs.title: Missing duration
docs.text:
If JUnit does not provide time, TestBudget records:

"duration_s": 0.0

instead of dropping the result.

docs.title: Building Playwright invocations
docs.text:
Read selected Playwright tests from plan.json:

from testbudget.adapters.playwright_adapter import (
    build_playwright_invocations,
)

invocations = build_playwright_invocations("plan.json")

Suppose the plan selects:

tests/checkout.spec.ts › checkout succeeds
tests/payment.spec.ts › payment succeeds
tests/checkout.spec.ts › checkout rejects card

TestBudget returns:

[
    {
        "file": "tests/checkout.spec.ts",
        "test_ids": [
            "tests/checkout.spec.ts › checkout succeeds",
            "tests/checkout.spec.ts › checkout rejects card",
        ],
        "titles": [
            "checkout succeeds",
            "checkout rejects card",
        ],
    },
    {
        "file": "tests/payment.spec.ts",
        "test_ids": [
            "tests/payment.spec.ts › payment succeeds",
        ],
        "titles": [
            "payment succeeds",
        ],
    },
]

docs.title: Why per-file invocation?
docs.text:
Playwright normally executes test files in parallel and does not guarantee execution order across files.

TestBudget therefore does not rely on passing one ordered list of test IDs to Playwright.

Instead, the adapter produces per-file invocation groups that the integration layer can execute deliberately.

docs.title: Mixed-framework plans
docs.text:
Plans may contain pytest and Playwright tests.

Pytest IDs use:

path::name

Playwright IDs use:

file › title

The Playwright adapter ignores pytest IDs.

docs.title: Invalid input
docs.text:
The adapter rejects:

  • missing JUnit files;
  • malformed XML;
  • testcases without usable files;
  • testcases without titles;
  • invalid durations;
  • missing plan files;
  • malformed plan JSON;
  • plans without a selected list.

docs.title: Pytest adapter
docs.text:
TestBudget's pytest adapter connects pytest execution to the shared TestBudget history and plan formats.

It provides two capabilities:

  1. normalize pytest JUnit output into TestBudget history records;
  2. execute only the pytest tests selected by plan.json, in plan order.

docs.title: Test identity
docs.text:
Pytest tests use the TestBudget identity:

path::name

Example:

tests/test_checkout.py::test_checkout_success

This identity is shared by history, links, ranking, replay, and execution.

docs.title: Parsing pytest JUnit
docs.text:
Generate a pytest JUnit report:

python -m pytest \
  --junitxml=test-results.xml

Parse it:

from testbudget.adapters.pytest_adapter import parse_pytest_junit

results = parse_pytest_junit("test-results.xml")

A result looks like:

{
  "test_id": "tests/test_checkout.py::test_checkout_success",
  "status": "passed",
  "duration_s": 1.21,
  "attempt": 1
}

The adapter accepts pytest xunit1 and xunit2 reports.

docs.title: xunit1
docs.text:
xunit1 commonly provides a file attribute directly.

For example:

<testcase
    classname="tests.test_checkout"
    name="test_checkout_success"
    file="tests/test_checkout.py"
    time="1.21"
/>

TestBudget uses the explicit file path.

docs.title: xunit2
docs.text:
xunit2 may omit file.

In that case TestBudget derives the path from the JUnit classname.

For example:

tests.test_checkout

becomes:

tests/test_checkout.py

A class-based classname such as:

tests.test_checkout.TestCheckout

also maps to:

tests/test_checkout.py

docs.title: Status normalization
docs.text:
TestBudget uses three result states:

passed
failed
skipped

JUnit <failure> and <error> are both recorded as:

failed

JUnit <skipped> becomes:

skipped

A testcase with none of those children is:

passed

docs.title: Missing duration
docs.text:
JUnit producers may omit the time attribute.

TestBudget stores such results as:

"duration_s": 0.0

instead of discarding the test result.

docs.title: Retry attempts
docs.text:
If the same test appears repeatedly in one JUnit report, TestBudget assigns attempt numbers:

attempt 1
attempt 2
attempt 3

The flake-filter stage can later use this information to detect failures that pass on retry.

docs.title: Running a TestBudget plan
docs.text:
Load the pytest adapter as a plugin:

python -m pytest \
  -p testbudget.adapters.pytest_adapter \
  --testbudget-plan plan.json

Suppose pytest normally collects:

test_alpha
test_beta
test_gamma

and plan.json selects:

{
  "selected": [
    {
      "test_id": "tests/test_example.py::test_gamma"
    },
    {
      "test_id": "tests/test_example.py::test_alpha"
    }
  ]
}

TestBudget changes collection to:

test_gamma
test_alpha

test_beta is reported as deselected.

This means TestBudget controls both:

  • which pytest tests run;
  • the order in which they run.

docs.title: Mixed-framework plans
docs.text:
A TestBudget plan can contain tests from multiple frameworks.

The pytest adapter only consumes pytest IDs using:

path::name

Playwright tests use a different identity format and are ignored by the pytest adapter.

docs.title: Running without TestBudget
docs.text:
If --testbudget-plan is not supplied, the plugin leaves pytest collection unchanged.

Normal pytest execution is preserved.

docs.title: Invalid plans
docs.text:
The adapter rejects:

  • missing plan files;
  • malformed JSON;
  • plans without a selected list;
  • selected entries without valid test_id values.

This avoids silently running an unintended set of tests.

docs.title: Plugin helper naming
docs.text:
Functions beginning with pytest_ are reserved for pytest hooks when a module is loaded as a plugin.

Internal TestBudget helper functions therefore avoid that prefix unless they implement a real pytest hook.

This prevents pluggy from attempting to register ordinary helper functions as pytest hooks.

docs.title: Preparing a release
docs.text:
1. Ensure the intended changes are merged into main.
  2. Run the test suite and lint checks.
  3. Review the changelog and update version information in pyproject.toml.
  4. Create a version tag using the project's agreed version, such as v0.1.0.
  5. Publish a GitHub Release with notes describing the changes.

docs.title: Archiving with Zenodo
docs.text:
1. Enable the repository integration in Zenodo using an authorized maintainer account.
  2. Verify that the repository is connected and that new GitHub Releases trigger archiving.
  3. Check that the archived record and DOI are available after the first release.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Release versions and publication should be agreed upon by project maintainers. Do not publish a release or claim a DOI exists until the process has been verified.

docs.title: What went well
docs.text:
• Breaking work into smaller changes made reviews easier.
  • Automated tests helped catch regressions.

docs.title: What could improve
docs.text:
• Run linting and tests before opening a pull request.
  • Keep documentation and the issue status log updated with each change.
  • Make PR descriptions clearly state what changed and how it was validated.

docs.title: Action items
docs.text:
• Run pytest and Ruff locally before submitting PRs.
  • Keep PRs focused and link them to their related issues.
  • Update the changelog and status log when appropriate.

docs.title: Reviewer overrides and audit mode
docs.text:
TestBudget normally executes only the tests selected by its budgeted plan.

Two mechanisms allow the team to collect more evidence safely:

  1. an authorized reviewer can request a full-suite run;
  2. audit mode can execute the full suite while preserving the plan TestBudget would have selected.

docs.title: Reviewer command
docs.text:
A reviewer can request the complete suite using:

/testbudget full

The command is accepted only when the comment author's resolved repository permission is:

write
maintain
admin

The following permissions are not sufficient:

read
triage

docs.title: Why permission checking is separate
docs.text:
The reviewer module does not call GitHub directly.

The GitHub integration resolves the comment author's repository permission and passes that value to TestBudget.

For example:

from testbudget.reviewer import (
    parse_reviewer_command,
)

command = parse_reviewer_command(
    "/testbudget full",
    actor_permission="write",
)

This keeps authorization logic deterministic and testable without requiring network access.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
A valid command returns:

{
    "action": "full",
}

An unrelated comment returns:

None

Unsupported TestBudget commands and unauthorized requests fail explicitly.

docs.title: Known test IDs
docs.text:
Reviewer-driven test IDs must already exist in TestBudget history.

Load known IDs with:

from testbudget.reviewer import (
    load_known_test_ids,
)

known = load_known_test_ids("history")

Validate requested IDs with:

from testbudget.reviewer import (
    validate_test_ids,
)

validated = validate_test_ids(
    requested_test_ids,
    known,
)

Unknown IDs are rejected instead of being forwarded to a test runner.

docs.title: Normal execution
docs.text:
Suppose TestBudget produces:

selected:
A
B

skipped:
C
D

Normal execution is:

A
B

docs.title: Audit mode
docs.text:
Audit mode preserves that plan but executes:

A
B
C
D

The original plan remains:

selected:
A
B

skipped:
C
D

This distinction matters because audit mode answers:

What would TestBudget have selected, and what did the full suite actually reveal?

If audit mode rewrote every test as selected, that evidence would be lost.

docs.title: Building an execution policy
docs.text:
from testbudget.audit import (
    build_execution_policy,
)

policy = build_execution_policy(
    plan,
    all_test_ids,
    audit_mode=True,
)

Example result:

{
    "mode": "audit",
    "audit_mode": True,
    "force_full": False,
    "execute_test_ids": [
        "A",
        "B",
        "C",
        "D",
    ],
    "planned_selected_test_ids": [
        "A",
        "B",
    ],
    "planned_skipped_test_ids": [
        "C",
        "D",
    ],
}

docs.title: Reviewer full-suite override
docs.text:
After parsing:

command = parse_reviewer_command(
    "/testbudget full",
    "write",
)

apply it using:

from testbudget.audit import (
    apply_reviewer_command,
)

policy = apply_reviewer_command(
    plan,
    all_test_ids,
    command,
)

The resulting mode is:

reviewer_full

and all known tests execute.

docs.title: Audit vs reviewer full
docs.text: Both modes execute the complete suite, but they express different intent.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
mode = audit

The project is deliberately collecting full-suite evidence while observing what TestBudget would have selected.

docs.title: Reviewer full
docs.text:
mode = reviewer_full

An authorized reviewer explicitly overrode budgeted selection.

Keeping the modes separate allows checks and evaluation reports to explain why the full suite ran.

docs.title: Integration responsibility
docs.text:
This module does not:

  • receive GitHub webhooks;
  • call the GitHub permission API;
  • post check runs;
  • execute pytest or Playwright itself.

Those integration layers consume the command and execution-policy objects.

This separation avoids coupling policy logic to GitHub networking and keeps the core behavior easy to test.
